article_sentences: Three months of lull established by security forces in Jammu and Kashmir was rattled by the back-to-back incidents of violence in the past six days.
On November 11, a terror attack on a checkpoint manned by the personnel of the Central Reserve.
Police Force (CRPF) in Kulgam left three jawans injured.
On November 16, a local, whom the police suspected of having joined the terror ranks a few days ago, was killed after six days of a siege-like anti-terror operation in residential areas of Kulgam.
In Jammu’s Kishtwar, two Special.
Police Officers (SPOs) of the J&K. Police were found dead with bullet wounds, a day after they were reported missing in a forest range on November 11.
The police and the Army, however, remain tight-lipped about the circumstances around the killing of these SPOs, and there are conflicting reports on the circumstances that led to their deaths.
The anti-terror operation in civilian areas of Kulgam has raised concerns.

Former J&K Chief Minister and PDP president Mehbooba Mufti described the operation, spread over six days, as “collective punishment that only breeds alienation and resentment,” while NC spokesman Imran Nabi Dar suggested that entire villages were put under prolonged restrictions for days.
The Omar Abdullah government, because of limited powers and no jurisdiction over the police in J&K, a Union Territory since 2019, finds itself hamstrung.
The iron hand policy to stamp out terrorism and separatism has been effective from a strictly security perspective — terror attacks as well as local recruitments into terror ranks have declined.
According to the police, local recruits have come down to single digit or fewer than 10 in Kashmir.

article_sentences: Even as Cyclone Akvan gathers strength over the Bay of Bengal, the Regional Meteorological Centre (RMC) here has forecast moderate rainfall at isolated places in Chennai, Tiruvallur and Chengalpattu districts on Wednesday.
Light rain is also likely at isolated places over south Tamil Nadu, the rest of north coastal Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal.
Dry weather is likely to prevail over the rest of the State.
For Thursday, the RMC has forecast heavy rain at isolated places in Chennai and Tiruvallur districts.
Moderate rain is likely at isolated places in Chengalpattu, Kanchipuram, Villupuram and Cuddalore districts, as well as in Puducherry.
Light rain is likely at isolated places over the Western Ghats districts.
Dry weather is likely to prevail over the rest of the State and Karaikal.
Meanwhile, Cyclone Akvan moved northwestwards and lay centred at 8.30 a.m. on Tuesday about 610 km east of Chennai.
It is very likely to move slowly north-northwestwards and intensify further into a severe cyclonic storm over the westcentral Bay of Bengal by the evening of November 17, 2026.
Thereafter, it is likely to move northwestwards and intensify into a very severe cyclonic storm by Thursday morning.
The system is likely to cross the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coasts between Nellore and Tuni around Thursday noon, with a maximum sustained wind speed of 120–130 kmph, gusting to 145 kmph.

stories.headline: Delhi building collapse: Two killed, five injured as 50-year-old Jwala Nagar structure gives way
stories.title: Delhi building collapse: Two killed, five injured as 50-year-old Jwala Nagar structure gives way
stories.summary: The three-year-old boy and a factory worker were among those killed; residents allege repeated complaints about the building’s deteriorating condition went unaddressed, while MCD flags possible role of railway vibrations
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'building collapse' in title weight 46
article_sentences: Two people, including a three-year-old boy, were killed and five others injured after a nearly 50-year-old building, housing a gajak factory on the ground floor and residential rooms above it, collapsed in east Delhi’s Jwala Nagar on Tuesday (November 17, 2026) morning, trapping people under the debris.
The owner of the property, identified as Surendar Singh, was subsequently arrested, after he switched off his mobile phone and tried to flee, DCP (Shahdara) R.P. Meena said.

An FIR has been registered under Sections 106(1) (Causing death by negligence), 125(A) (Causing hurt by a rash or negligent act endangering life or safety) and 223 (Disobedience to an order duly promulgated by a public servant) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS).
Mr. Meena said Section 223 was added to the FIR as the owner did not verify the tenants staying in his property.
The collapse, which brought down the right portion of the building in a congested residential lane, left a heap of bricks, iron girders and household belongings where the structure had stood.

Residents said they had repeatedly raised concerns about the building’s deteriorating condition, pointing to leaking roof, cracks in its walls and metal girders and other structural elements becoming exposed, but alleged that the owner had not undertaken the necessary repairs.
The deceased were identified as Devansh alias Laddu (3), and Pintu (32).
The injured were identified as Devansh’s mother Khushbu (30), Vikesh (30), Akash (27), Dalip (26), Aman alias Dosa (32).
All six were taken to Dr. Hedgewar Hospital, where Devansh and Pintu were declared brought dead, while the injured were admitted for treatment.
The incident was reported around 10.09 a.m. in Gali No. 6, near Peer Baba Mazar in the Sabji Mandi area.
A distress call was received at Vivek Vihar police station, following which police personnel rushed to the spot and initiated rescue operations.
The Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD), meanwhile, recorded receiving the incident call at 10.25 a.m.

stories.headline: Reel Makers Not Entitled To Journalistic Protection During Protests, Delhi Police To Supreme Court
stories.title: Reel Makers Not Entitled To Journalistic Protection During Protests, Delhi Police To Supreme Court
stories.summary: It has to be determined if reel-makers and content-creators can be elevated to the status of journalists, the Delhi police said.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: It has to be determined if reel-makers and content-creators can be elevated to the status of journalists, the Delhi police said.

The Delhi Police has told the Supreme Court that its order directing protection of journalists covering the anti-Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) protests was not intended to cover "so-called reel makers and social media influencers".
In a counter-affidavit filed before the Supreme Court, the Delhi.

Police said that some participants in the "illegal protests" were content creators making YouTube reels while carrying cameras and microphones, making it difficult for police personnel to distinguish between genuine journalists and reel-makers on the ground.

The police said that it had to be determined whether "reel-makers can be elevated to the status of journalists or reporters", adding that the distinction was highlighted only to explain the practical difficulties faced by police personnel while managing protests.
Clarifying that it did not intend to obstruct content creators from pursuing their activities, the Delhi.

Police said that the guidelines for journalists covering protests were meant to distinguish professional journalists and reporters from persons carrying cameras and microphones for other purposes, including commercial exploitation of content.
The affidavit was filed by Joint Commissioner of Police Surrender Kumar on behalf of the Delhi.

Police responding to the petitions filed by the Network of Women in Media, Free Speech Collective, Delhi Union of Journalists and the Kerala Union of Working Journalists concerning alleged police misconduct against journalists covering the protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

The police referred to the Supreme Court's order dated October 11, 2026, which recorded the assurance given by the Solicitor General that lawyers, journalists and other professionals would not be hindered in discharging their professional duties.

It submitted that the direction was intended to protect journalists in the discharge of their professional duties and was not meant to exempt reel-makers, social media influencers or unruly elements from the general law or lawful directions of law enforcement agencies at the site of a prohibited assembly.

The affidavit further stated that the police had not placed any restriction on the right of citizens to report or disseminate information, nor had anyone been proceeded against merely for lacking press accreditation or an identity card.

stories.headline: CM Chandrababu Naidu seeks Centre bailout as 2 cyclones cost AP Rs 7k cr
stories.title: CM Chandrababu Naidu seeks Centre bailout as 2 cyclones cost AP Rs 7k cr
stories.summary: Naidu meets FM in Delhi, discusses cyclone damage Farm losses, battered coastal infra figure in talks Seeks funds for Rayalaseema Horticulture Hub, VER
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Amaravati: Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu has appealed to Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman for immediate financial assistance to Andhra Pradesh, which suffered losses exceeding Rs 7,000 crore due to two successive cyclones, Arnav and Murasu, affecting agriculture, coastal infrastructure and other sectors.

During his visit to New Delhi on Tuesday, Naidu met Sitharaman and discussed the state's financial situation, cyclone damage, the Rayalaseema Horticulture Hub, release of Purvodaya funds, region-specific development plans and key decisions announced at the recent CII Partnership Summit in Visakhapatnam.
The Chief Minister explained that preliminary estimates put the combined losses from the two cyclones at over Rs 7,000 crore.
Crops ready for harvest were submerged in floodwaters, severely affecting farmers.
He briefed her on the precautionary measures taken before the cyclones and subsequent relief and restoration operations.
Despite the impact of El Nino, the state had ensured irrigation water supply to several areas through the Pattiseema project.
However, the cyclones dealt a severe blow to farmers.
Coastal infrastructure and, particularly, the power distribution network also suffered extensive damage.

Naidu said Central teams had already visited the state to assess the losses and requested immediate assistance without waiting for prolonged delays, stating that early financial support would help accelerate relief and restoration.
The Chief Minister also outlined region-specific development strategies for Visakhapatnam, Amaravati and Tirupati to drive economic growth.

Regarding the Rayalaseema Horticulture Hub, for which Sitharaman had earlier laid the foundation stone, he sought funds for infrastructure, rural road connectivity, irrigation facilities and promotion of drip irrigation.
He also requested additional Central assistance for the Visakhapatnam Economic Region, which is witnessing rapid growth, to accelerate development and ensure its benefits reach the people.

stories.headline: How Youth and Communities Are Coming Together to Protect Kashmir's Vital Water Commons
stories.title: How Youth and Communities Are Coming Together to Protect Kashmir's Vital Water Commons
stories.summary: River Jhelum, Foot Bridge Srinagar Submerged ankle-deep in the muddy shallows of the Jhelum, Nayeem Farooq pulled a tangled plastic sheet from the water and dropped it into the growing pile beside him. The B-Tech student from Baramulla had begun cleaning the river only two months earlier. Behind him, volunteers carried sacks of waste up the slippery embankment. For Farooq, the river was no longer just a waterway at the edge of town; it had become a responsibility he could no longer ignore. Nayeem farooq and his team collecting the garbage from the Jhelum in polythenes “The Day the Jhelum Became Personal” “I and my cousin were once sitting on the banks of the Jhelum in Baramulla when he went for a swim in the river. But when he returned, his eyes had turned red. Concerned, I asked him what had happened, and he told me that the polluted water had caused irritation and infection. What seemed like an ordinary moment soon became a deeply disturbing experience for me. I could not stop thinking about how a river that sustains an entire town was being pushed towards such neglect”, Nayeem said. “As I began observing its condition more closely, I came across heaps of garbage, discarded diapers and even dead animals dumped into the water. It was heartbreaking to see a river that people depend on for their drinking water being reduced to a dumping ground. I kept wondering how we could allow the very water body that sustains our lives to become a threat to our health. For nearly one-and-a-half years, I had been appealing to people through social media to stop polluting the Jhelum, but the response was far from encouraging. I eventually realised that words alone would not bring change; I had to step forward myself, take responsibility and set an example. That realisation became the beginning of my journey to clean and protect the Jhelum.” Jhelum is Kashmir’s lifeline, supplying drinking water and irrigation while also protecting the Valley from floods. But unchecked pollution, encroachment, and weak conservation have steadily weakened these functions. Originating at Verinag, the river collects water from streams including the Lidder, Veshav, and Rambiara before draining into Wular Lake and flowing out of the Valley. Drains from south to north Kashmir discharge directly into it, while solid waste dumping and illegal sand mining damage its ecology. The loss of wetlands and floodplains has also reduced its capacity to absorb excess water, leaving the Jhelum increasingly vulnerable to flooding after sustained rain. Jhelum Clean Drive: From One Volunteer to a Community Movement Shahida (name changed), a resident of Baramulla, proudly recalled, “While dropping my children to school one morning, I saw Nayeem Farooq and his team cleaning the Jhelum. My children noticed them and asked me what they were doing. I explained that they were cleaning the river to keep our environment clean and protect the water we drink. I was happy to see their curiosity, and they later started sharing the message with their classmates, telling them why it is important to keep our rivers clean. The impact of this initiative is also visible at home. My children no longer tolerate garbage lying around in our garden or inside the house. They make sure everything is kept clean. This initiative has taught them that cleanliness is not just about keeping our homes clean but also about taking responsibility for our surroundings. I feel that when children learn to care for nature at such a young age, they become agents of change and inspire others to do the same.” “I had been raising awareness about river pollution for nearly one-and-a-half years before launching the Jhelum Clean Drive around two-and-a-half months ago. What began as an individual effort has gradually brought together a group of 60 to 75 volunteers, including nearly 35 to 40 women, most of them young people,” Nayeem Farooq said. “Together, we have collected around 11.5 tonnes of garbage from one stretch of the river in Baramulla and transported it to a designated municipal dumping site. The Municipal Council has also extended support to our efforts. Alongside the clean-up drives, we conduct awareness campaigns through social media and local mosques especially on Friday sermons, urging people not to use the river as a dustbin.” “However, cleaning the visible garbage is only the beginning. I am equally concerned about the waste entering the Jhelum through drainage pipes, particularly from butcher shops and other commercial establishments along its banks. Even after cleaning a stretch, I often return the following day to find fresh garbage dumped at the same spot, which can be disheartening. Yet, I believe change takes time and sustained community participation. I have also approached the Deputy Commissioner Baramulla, SyeedFakhrudin Hamid, with an application seeking measures to prevent garbage dumping along the riverbanks and bridges. My aim is not to restrict this initiative to Baramulla; I want to extend it to Srinagar and other parts of Kashmir and work towards protecting our rivers and waterbodies,” he added. Beyond Awareness: Youth Taking Action to Protect Jhelum's Water Commons For Mehak Khursheed, the Jhelum is more than just a river; it is a shared common resource that everyone has a responsibility to protect. A Radio Uri RJ, social activist and hotel management graduate, Mehak travelled from Uri to Baramulla to join Nayeem Farooq’s cleanliness drive, believing that protecting water commons is a collective responsibility that goes beyond geographical boundaries and begins with individual action. Mehak removing the plastic trash from the River Jhelum Since the drive began, I have noticed a positive response. People have started calling me, asking about the initiative and expressing their willingness to participate. I travelled from Uri to Baramulla because I believe protecting the Jhelum is not just the responsibility of Baramulla residents; it belongs to all of us. Just as we keep our homes clean, we must protect our rivers. The government should also install dustbins, put up warning boards and impose fines on those who throw garbage into the river. Awareness is important, but without accountability, lasting change will be difficult. For SadiyaJaved, protecting the Jhelum is not just an environmental concern but a responsibility that the younger generation must embrace. A B.Sc. Biochemistry student from Baramulla, Sadiya joined Nayeem Farooq’s Jhelum Clean Drive after learning about it through social media. She believes awareness must translate into action and that greater public and government participation is essential to protecting Kashmir’s water commons. Sadiya on Jhelum Cleanliness Drive “There is no shortage of awareness in Kashmir, but what we lack is action on the ground. During the drive, we received both appreciation and criticism on social media. Some people questioned what difference a few volunteers could make by collecting garbage, but that did not discourage us. Our efforts also encouraged other people to join the cleaning activities. The government has appreciated our initiative, but we have not received any significant support. If the Municipal Council and the administration actively joined hands with us, the impact could be much greater,” Impact of Climate Change on Jhelum Farooq Ahmed, Executive Engineer, Flood Control Department Kashmir Explains, “Climate change is altering rainfall patterns in Kashmir. Instead of prolonged rainfall, we are increasingly witnessing short-duration, intense rainfall and cloudbursts, leading to sudden fluctuations in water levels, particularly in the Jhelum's tributaries. The Jhelum basin is surrounded by mountainous catchment areas, and water from several tributaries eventually flows into the river, putting pressure on its carrying capacity. We need to treat these catchment areas and restore floodplains and flood basins to better manage flood risks.” “Another major concern is illegal sand mining, which is gradually weakening the river's embankments,” Farooq Ahmed said. “People extract sand from the river, often under the cover of darkness, and in the process damage the flood-protection structures. We do not permit official mining in the Jhelum under our jurisdiction, but illegal extraction remains a challenge. Protecting the river requires collective efforts, strict enforcement and public cooperation.” According to a study “ Assessment and interpretation of surface water quality in Jhelum River and its tributaries using multivariate statistical methods” published in Environmental Monitoring and Assessment reveals water quality in the Jhelum River and its tributaries in the Kashmir Himalayas is consistently deteriorating. The researchers tested 14 physico-chemical parameters at 26 sites across all four seasons and found that the upstream Jhelum was least polluted, while Nallah Sindh had the poorest water quality. They reported that the Jhelum and Wular Lake were strongly affected by pollution from adjoining tributaries, and that chemical, conventional, and organic pollutants were key factors influencing the river’s condition. The study concluded that its findings could help guide the sustainable management of Kashmir’s surface-water resources and protect the region’s fragile ecology. Govt Backs the Initiative Manzoor Moazin, Sanitation Supervisor, Municipal Council Baramulla, said. “We regularly organise cleanliness drives, dedicating an hour to cleaning different areas. We also involve self-help groups, conduct awareness programmes and deploy cleanliness vehicles to maintain sanitation across the town. However, public participation, particularly in Old Town Baramulla and densely populated areas, remains a challenge. There is a need to develop a stronger sense of civic responsibility so that cleanliness becomes a daily habit rather than remaining limited to official drives. I appreciate Nayeem Farooq's efforts and have also been actively participating in his cleanliness campaign. Such initiatives, supported by public participation and government efforts, can bring lasting change in how we protect our rivers and shared spaces.” (The author is a recipient of the Promise of Commons Fellowship 2026, on the significance of Commons and its community stewardship)

I was happy to see their curiosity, and they later started sharing the message with their classmates, telling them why it is important to keep our rivers clean.
The impact of this initiative is also visible at home.
My children no longer tolerate garbage lying around in our garden or inside the house.
They make sure everything is kept clean.
This initiative has taught them that cleanliness is not just about keeping our homes clean but also about taking responsibility for our surroundings.

I feel that when children learn to care for nature at such a young age, they become agents of change and inspire others to do the same.” “I had been raising awareness about river pollution for nearly one-and-a-half years before launching the Jhelum Clean Drive around two-and-a-half months ago.
What began as an individual effort has gradually brought together a group of 60 to 75 volunteers, including nearly 35 to 40 women, most of them young people,” Nayeem Farooq said.
“Together, we have collected around 11.5 tonnes of garbage from one stretch of the river in Baramulla and transported it to a designated municipal dumping site.
The Municipal Council has also extended support to our efforts.

Alongside the clean-up drives, we conduct awareness campaigns through social media and local mosques especially on Friday sermons, urging people not to use the river as a dustbin.” “However, cleaning the visible garbage is only the beginning.
I am equally concerned about the waste entering the Jhelum through drainage pipes, particularly from butcher shops and other commercial establishments along its banks.
Even after cleaning a stretch, I often return the following day to find fresh garbage dumped at the same spot, which can be disheartening.
Yet, I believe change takes time and sustained community participation.
I have also approached the Deputy Commissioner Baramulla, SyeedFakhrudin Hamid, with an application seeking measures to prevent garbage dumping along the riverbanks and bridges.
My aim is not to restrict this initiative to Baramulla; I want to extend it to Srinagar and other parts of Kashmir and work towards protecting our rivers and waterbodies,” he added.

Beyond Awareness: Youth Taking Action to Protect Jhelum's Water Commons For Mehak Khursheed, the Jhelum is more than just a river; it is a shared common resource that everyone has a responsibility to protect.

A Radio Uri RJ, social activist and hotel management graduate, Mehak travelled from Uri to Baramulla to join Nayeem Farooq’s cleanliness drive, believing that protecting water commons is a collective responsibility that goes beyond geographical boundaries and begins with individual action.
Mehak removing the plastic trash from the River Jhelum.
Since the drive began, I have noticed a positive response.
People have started calling me, asking about the initiative and expressing their willingness to participate.
I travelled from Uri to Baramulla because I believe protecting the Jhelum is not just the responsibility of Baramulla residents; it belongs to all of us.
Just as we keep our homes clean, we must protect our rivers.
The government should also install dustbins, put up warning boards and impose fines on those who throw garbage into the river.
Awareness is important, but without accountability, lasting change will be difficult.
For SadiyaJaved, protecting the Jhelum is not just an environmental concern but a responsibility that the younger generation must embrace.
A B.Sc.
Biochemistry student from Baramulla, Sadiya joined Nayeem Farooq’s Jhelum Clean Drive after learning about it through social media.
She believes awareness must translate into action and that greater public and government participation is essential to protecting Kashmir’s water commons.
Sadiya on Jhelum Cleanliness Drive “There is no shortage of awareness in Kashmir, but what we lack is action on the ground.
During the drive, we received both appreciation and criticism on social media.
Some people questioned what difference a few volunteers could make by collecting garbage, but that did not discourage us.
Our efforts also encouraged other people to join the cleaning activities.
The government has appreciated our initiative, but we have not received any significant support.

If the Municipal Council and the administration actively joined hands with us, the impact could be much greater,” Impact of Climate Change on Jhelum Farooq Ahmed, Executive Engineer, Flood Control Department Kashmir Explains, “Climate change is altering rainfall patterns in Kashmir.

Instead of prolonged rainfall, we are increasingly witnessing short-duration, intense rainfall and cloudbursts, leading to sudden fluctuations in water levels, particularly in the Jhelum's tributaries.
The Jhelum basin is surrounded by mountainous catchment areas, and water from several tributaries eventually flows into the river, putting pressure on its carrying capacity.

We need to treat these catchment areas and restore floodplains and flood basins to better manage flood risks.” “Another major concern is illegal sand mining, which is gradually weakening the river's embankments,” Farooq Ahmed said.
“People extract sand from the river, often under the cover of darkness, and in the process damage the flood-protection structures.
We do not permit official mining in the Jhelum under our jurisdiction, but illegal extraction remains a challenge.

Protecting the river requires collective efforts, strict enforcement and public cooperation.” According to a study “ Assessment and interpretation of surface water quality in Jhelum River and its tributaries using multivariate statistical methods” published in Environmental Monitoring and Assessment reveals water quality in the Jhelum River and its tributaries in the Kashmir Himalayas is consistently deteriorating.
The researchers tested 14 physico-chemical parameters at 26 sites across all four seasons and found that the upstream Jhelum was least polluted, while Nallah Sindh had the poorest water quality.

They reported that the Jhelum and Wular Lake were strongly affected by pollution from adjoining tributaries, and that chemical, conventional, and organic pollutants were key factors influencing the river’s condition.
The study concluded that its findings could help guide the sustainable management of Kashmir’s surface-water resources and protect the region’s fragile ecology.
Govt Backs the Initiative Manzoor Moazin, Sanitation Supervisor, Municipal Council Baramulla, said.
“We regularly organise cleanliness drives, dedicating an hour to cleaning different areas.
We also involve self-help groups, conduct awareness programmes and deploy cleanliness vehicles to maintain sanitation across the town.
However, public participation, particularly in Old Town Baramulla and densely populated areas, remains a challenge.
There is a need to develop a stronger sense of civic responsibility so that cleanliness becomes a daily habit rather than remaining limited to official drives.
I appreciate Nayeem Farooq's efforts and have also been actively participating in his cleanliness campaign.

Such initiatives, supported by public participation and government efforts, can bring lasting change in how we protect our rivers and shared spaces.” (The author is a recipient of the Promise of Commons Fellowship 2026, on the significance of Commons and its community stewardship).

stories.headline: India’s GDP growth pegged at 7.3% in FY26-27, may touch 7.7% next quarter: EAC-PM Chairman
stories.title: India’s GDP growth pegged at 7.3% in FY26-27, may touch 7.7% next quarter: EAC-PM Chairman
stories.summary: EAC-PM chair says exports, FDI revival and micro-entrepreneurship drive trajectory as India targets $1 trillion in exports in 2026-27 amid steady growth outlook
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: India’s GDP growth is likely to reach 7.3 per cent during the current financial year, with the economy projected to grow at around 7.7 per cent in the next quarter, S Mahendra Dev, Chairman of the Economic Advisory Council to the Prime Minister (EAC-PM), said on Tuesday.

Speaking to ANI on the sidelines of the JRD TATA Awards 2026, Dev expressed confidence in the country's economic outlook, citing sustained export momentum, diversification of export markets and improving foreign investment inflows as key contributors to growth.
"India’s growth we are expecting 7.3 per cent this year.
And then next quarter, about 7.7 per cent," Dev said in response to a question by ANI.
On the country's export outlook, Dev said India's export momentum was expected to remain strong throughout the financial year, supported by diversification of export destinations.
He said the country was targeting $1 trillion in exports in FY 2026-27.
"We have diversified the exports.
So, I think it will be there throughout the year, and we are planning for $1 trillion exports this year, FY 2026-27," he said.
He further expressed confidence that the positive export performance recorded between April and September, as well as in October, would continue in November and the subsequent months.
On foreign investment, Dev said foreign direct investment (FDI) was returning to India, while foreign portfolio investment (FPI) was also witnessing renewed inflows.
He emphasised that foreign capital would complement domestic investment and help strengthen the country's export capacity.
